notes: 20 items: 3 lifted-style, 17 fresh. Identify London (dispersion), dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding interactions in given compounds from structure.

items.question: Name the THREE types of intermolecular forces (IMFs) covered in CAPS Physical Sciences.
items.expectedAnswer: (1) LONDON forces (also called dispersion forces or instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces); (2) DIPOLE-DIPOLE forces (between permanent dipoles in polar molecules); (3) HYDROGEN BONDING (a special, strong dipole-dipole between an H attached to N, O or F and another N/O/F).
items.explanation: London (in all molecules), dipole-dipole (polar molecules), hydrogen bonding (H attached to N/O/F).

items.question: Identify the strongest intermolecular force present in liquid H₂O.
items.expectedAnswer: Hydrogen bonding
items.explanation: H is bonded to O (an N/O/F atom) ⇒ hydrogen bonding possible. H-bonding is the strongest of the three IMFs present in water.

items.question: What intermolecular forces are present in liquid CH₄ (methane)?
items.expectedAnswer: Only LONDON (dispersion) forces. CH₄ is a non-polar molecule (symmetric tetrahedral C-H bonds, no net dipole) — so no dipole-dipole forces. H is bonded to C (not N/O/F) — so no hydrogen bonding. Just London forces between methane molecules.
items.explanation: Non-polar tetrahedral methane: London only.

items.question: What intermolecular forces are present in liquid HCl?
items.expectedAnswer: London forces AND dipole-dipole forces. HCl is a POLAR molecule (Cl is more electronegative than H, so the molecule has a permanent dipole). However, H is bonded to Cl (not N/O/F), so NO hydrogen bonding.
items.explanation: Polar molecules have London + dipole-dipole. H-bonding requires H on N/O/F — Cl doesn't qualify in CAPS.

items.question: What intermolecular forces are present in liquid NH₃ (ammonia)?
items.expectedAnswer: London + dipole-dipole + HYDROGEN BONDING. NH₃ is polar (N pulls electron density), and H is bonded to N — so hydrogen bonding occurs (N-H...N type).
items.explanation: Polar + H bonded to N ⇒ all three IMFs. H-bonding is the strongest.

items.question: A student says: 'All POLAR molecules have hydrogen bonding.' Is this correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect. Polar molecules have dipole-dipole forces. Hydrogen bonding additionally requires an H atom bonded DIRECTLY to N, O, or F. For example, HCl is polar but does not have H-bonding (H is on Cl, not N/O/F). H₂S is polar but does not H-bond (H is on S).
items.explanation: Polar ⇒ dipole-dipole. H-bonding requires the H-on-N/O/F structural feature in addition.

items.question: A student says: 'Non-polar molecules don't have any intermolecular forces.' Is this correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect. ALL molecules (polar or non-polar) have LONDON (dispersion) forces. These arise from temporary fluctuations in electron distribution. Polar molecules ADDITIONALLY have dipole-dipole; H-bonders have H-bonding too. But London is universal.
items.explanation: London is in EVERY molecule. Non-polar molecules have only London (no dipole-dipole or H-bonding).

items.question: Identify the IMFs present in each: (a) Cl₂; (b) H₂O; (c) CH₃OH; (d) CO₂.
items.expectedAnswer: (a) Cl₂: London only (non-polar, symmetric); (b) H₂O: London + dipole-dipole + hydrogen bonding (H on O); (c) CH₃OH (methanol): London + dipole-dipole + hydrogen bonding (H on O of -OH); (d) CO₂: London only (linear, non-polar — although C=O bonds are polar, the symmetric linear shape cancels the net dipole).
items.explanation: Check polarity (shape matters!) + check H on N/O/F. CO₂ is a classic non-polar despite polar bonds.

items.question: Which of the following CAN form hydrogen bonds with itself: CH₃OH, CH₃Br, CH₃F, CH₃NH₂, CH₃COOH?
items.expectedAnswer: CH₃OH (alcohol; H on O), CH₃NH₂ (amine; H on N), and CH₃COOH (carboxylic acid; H on O of -COOH) can form H-bonds. CH₃Br: H bonded to C, not N/O/F. CH₃F: H bonded to C (the F is not bonded to H); doesn't H-bond with itself, although CH₃F can ACCEPT H-bonds from H-bond donors via F.
items.explanation: H-bond donor needs H bonded to N/O/F. Check each structure for such an H.

items.question: Which intermolecular force is the WEAKEST in general?
items.expectedAnswer: London (dispersion)
items.explanation: Strength ranking: H-bonding > dipole-dipole > London (within similar molecular sizes). London is the weakest per pair of molecules, BUT for large non-polar molecules, total London can be larger than dipole-dipole on smaller polar molecules.

items.question: Why do LONDON forces increase in strength as the molecule grows larger?
items.expectedAnswer: London forces arise from temporary, instantaneous dipoles created by electron movement. Larger molecules have MORE electrons (more polarisable) AND more SURFACE AREA for contact between molecules ⇒ stronger and more numerous temporary dipoles ⇒ stronger London forces overall.
items.explanation: More electrons + more surface contact ⇒ stronger London. Long alkanes can have very strong total London despite being non-polar.

items.question: Determine the IMFs in liquid CH₃CHO (ethanal/acetaldehyde).
items.expectedAnswer: London + dipole-dipole. The C=O bond is polar (O more electronegative than C), and the asymmetric shape gives a net dipole, so the molecule is polar. However, the H atoms are bonded to C, NOT to N/O/F, so NO hydrogen bonding (in the classical sense).
items.explanation: Aldehyde: polar (C=O dipole), but no H-on-O so no H-bonding.

items.question: Why does HF form unusually strong hydrogen bonds?
items.expectedAnswer: F is the most electronegative atom; the H-F bond is very polar (H carries a large δ+ and F a large δ−). This creates very strong attraction between F (with its lone pairs) on one molecule and the H on another. So H-bonding in HF is exceptionally strong, leading to HF's anomalously high boiling point (~20°C) for a small molecule.
items.explanation: Strongest electronegativity difference + small atomic size of F ⇒ very strong H-bonds.

items.question: Identify the IMFs present between two molecules of CH₃OCH₃ (dimethyl ether).
items.expectedAnswer: London + dipole-dipole. The C-O-C structure has a net dipole (O carries δ−, the alkyl C's have δ+), so the molecule is polar ⇒ dipole-dipole. The H atoms are bonded to C, not to O directly — so NO hydrogen bonding within ether molecules. (Note: ethers can act as H-bond ACCEPTORS for water etc., but pure ether doesn't self-H-bond.)
items.explanation: Ether: polar molecule, but no H-on-O ⇒ no self-H-bonding. London + dipole-dipole.

items.question: A learner draws a hydrogen bond between two CH₃Cl molecules. Is this correct? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect. CH₃Cl is a polar molecule, but the H atoms are bonded to C (not to N/O/F). Hydrogen bonding requires an H directly bonded to N, O, or F. So CH₃Cl does NOT form hydrogen bonds; only London + dipole-dipole interactions are present.
items.explanation: H-on-Cl or H-on-C doesn't qualify for H-bonding in CAPS.

items.question: List the IMFs in propan-1-ol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH).
items.expectedAnswer: London + dipole-dipole + HYDROGEN BONDING. The -OH group provides H bonded to O ⇒ H-bonding. The molecule is also polar ⇒ dipole-dipole. London forces present in all molecules.
items.explanation: Alcohol: -OH ⇒ H-bonding capable. All three IMFs present.

items.question: Why does CO₂ (linear) have NO net dipole moment despite having polar C=O bonds?
items.expectedAnswer: CO₂ has TWO C=O bond dipoles pointing in OPPOSITE directions (O=C=O linear structure). The two dipoles CANCEL each other vectorially, giving zero net dipole moment. So CO₂ is a NON-POLAR molecule despite having polar bonds.
items.explanation: Symmetry can cancel bond dipoles. Linear CO₂: O=C=O bonds opposite ⇒ cancel.

items.question: Which has STRONGER intermolecular forces: CH₃CH₂CH₃ (propane) or CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol)?
items.expectedAnswer: Ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) has stronger IMFs. Both molecules are similar in size (London forces are comparable). Propane has only London. Ethanol additionally has dipole-dipole AND hydrogen bonding (from -OH). H-bonding is much stronger than London, so ethanol has overall stronger IMFs ⇒ much higher boiling point (~78°C vs −42°C).
items.explanation: H-bonding dominates between molecules of similar size. Ethanol > propane in IMF strength.

items.question: True or False: 'A small polar molecule (like HCl) has stronger IMFs than a long non-polar molecule (like decane, C₁₀H₂₂).' Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: FALSE. While HCl has dipole-dipole forces in addition to London, decane is a much LARGER molecule with many more electrons and much more surface area for London contact. Long-chain non-polar molecules can have very strong CUMULATIVE London forces — often stronger than the IMFs of small polar molecules. This is why decane (BP ≈ 174°C) has a much higher BP than HCl (BP ≈ −85°C).
items.explanation: Size of London matters: cumulative London on a long chain can outweigh dipole-dipole on a small polar molecule.

items.question: Why does HF have a higher boiling point than HCl, despite Cl being heavier than F?
items.expectedAnswer: HF can form HYDROGEN BONDS (H bonded to F, a small electronegative atom). HCl has only London + dipole-dipole (Cl doesn't qualify for H-bonding under CAPS). H-bonding in HF is much stronger than the IMFs in HCl, so more energy is needed to vaporise HF ⇒ higher BP. (HF BP ≈ 20°C; HCl BP ≈ −85°C.)
items.explanation: H-bonding in HF >> London + dipole-dipole in HCl. H-bonding wins despite HF being smaller.
